body:
What is energy security?

Energy is essential for agriculture, industry, transport, communication and household activities. Electricity operates irrigation pumps, hospitals and communication systems. Petroleum fuels much of the transport sector, while gas, coal and other energy sources serve industries and households. An interruption in energy supply can therefore affect both economic production and daily life.

Energy security means the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price. In a broader sense, it also requires that people can obtain and use energy reliably, safely and in an environmentally and socially acceptable manner.

Energy security is not limited to possessing large reserves of coal, petroleum or natural gas. A country must also be able to extract or import energy, transport it to consumers, maintain the necessary infrastructure and manage changes in demand and prices.

The four As of energy security

The four As framework is a widely used method for examining different dimensions of energy security. It distinguishes physical supply from access, cost and social acceptance.

DimensionMeaningIllustration
AvailabilitySufficient energy resources and supply are available when required.A power system has enough generation and fuel to meet demand.
AccessibilityConsumers can obtain energy through suitable physical, commercial and institutional arrangements.A remote village has a functioning electricity connection.
AffordabilityEnergy prices are manageable for households, enterprises and the wider economy.A household can pay for essential electricity without sacrificing basic needs.
AcceptabilityEnergy production and use are compatible with environmental requirements and reasonable social concerns.A project addresses pollution, land-use impacts and affected communities.

These dimensions are related but not identical. A village may be connected to an electricity network but experience frequent interruptions. In that case, physical access exists, yet reliable availability is inadequate. Similarly, electricity may be continuously supplied but remain unaffordable for low-income households.

Energy security, electricity security and energy independence

Energy security covers all major forms of energy, including electricity, liquid fuels, gas and fuels used directly for heating or cooking. Electricity security concerns the ability of the power system to provide electricity reliably despite normal fluctuations and disturbances. It is therefore an important part of energy security, but not the entire subject.

Energy independence means relying little or not at all on imported energy. It is different from energy security. A country may import substantial quantities of fuel yet maintain secure supplies through diverse suppliers, dependable infrastructure, adequate reserves and international trade arrangements. Conversely, a country relying mainly on domestic energy may still face shortages because of droughts, mine disruptions or inadequate infrastructure.

Short-term and long-term security

In the short term, energy security requires the ability to withstand sudden disturbances such as fuel shipment delays, equipment failures or extreme weather. In the long term, it requires sufficient investment, resource management, technological development and adaptation to changing demand.

Energy efficiency strengthens both dimensions. When an efficient appliance provides the same lighting or cooling service using less energy, it reduces demand without necessarily reducing the service received by the consumer.

Prelims focus

  • Energy security concerns uninterrupted energy availability at an affordable price.
  • The four As are availability, accessibility, affordability and acceptability.
  • Electricity security is a component of broader energy security.
  • Energy efficiency can improve security by reducing energy required for the same service.
  • Trap: Energy security and complete freedom from energy imports are not synonymous.

[International Energy Agency, Glossary, entries on Energy Security, Energy Mix and Energy Service, consulted 16 November 2026; Asia Pacific Energy Research Centre, APEC Energy Demand and Supply Outlook, 7th edition, Volume I, Chapter 8, p. 144; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 8, Infrastructure, section 8.5, Energy, printed pp. 144–146.]

title: Energy Security: Meaning, the Four As and Energy Access

body:
Why energy supplies become insecure

Energy supply can be interrupted by natural disasters, conflicts, trade restrictions, accidents, infrastructure failures or sudden increases in demand. These risks operate at different stages of the supply chain. A country may possess sufficient fuel reserves but lack the infrastructure to deliver them, or it may have adequate generating stations but experience shortages of the fuel needed to operate them.

Energy resources are also unevenly distributed. Geological conditions determine the location of coal, petroleum and natural gas deposits. Solar and wind potential depend on climate and geography, while hydropower depends on suitable water resources and terrain. Consequently, energy production, transport and trade are closely connected to resource locations.

Indian resource locations and their significance

India has important coal-bearing regions in eastern and central parts of the country. Examples include Jharia in Jharkhand, Talcher in Odisha and Korba in Chhattisgarh. These locations illustrate how industrial activity and energy infrastructure may become concentrated around particular resources.

Domestic production strengthens supply options, but no resource is completely free from risk. Coal movement can be affected by transport disruptions. Hydropower output can vary with rainfall and reservoir conditions. Solar generation changes with sunlight, and wind generation changes with wind conditions. Petroleum and gas supply also depends on production, storage, transportation and, where relevant, imports.

What does diversification mean?

Energy diversification means reducing excessive dependence on any single fuel, supplier, location, transport route or technology. It does not necessarily mean using every available energy source in equal proportions.

  • Diversification of fuels: Using a suitable combination of coal, petroleum, natural gas, hydropower, solar, wind, nuclear energy and other sources according to their roles and limitations.
  • Diversification of suppliers: Obtaining imported fuels from more than one dependable source where feasible.
  • Diversification of transport routes: Reducing vulnerability to disruption of a single port, pipeline or shipping route.
  • Geographical diversification: Developing production and supply infrastructure across suitable locations rather than concentrating everything at one site.
  • Diversification through demand reduction: Improving efficiency and using alternatives that reduce dependence on a vulnerable fuel.

For example, if a country imports all its natural gas from one supplier, a disruption affecting that supplier can create a serious shortage. Importing from several suppliers may reduce this concentration risk. However, diversified contracts alone will not ensure security if all shipments must pass through the same vulnerable transport route.

Gujarat's role in energy supply

Gujarat's coastline gives it an important role in India's petroleum and natural gas infrastructure. The Dahej LNG terminal in Bharuch district receives imported liquefied natural gas, which is converted back into gaseous form for onward use. Such infrastructure creates an additional means of obtaining natural gas, but the fuel remains dependent on international supply arrangements.

Petronet LNG reported on 1 April 2026 that an expansion of its Dahej terminal from 17.5 million metric tonnes per annum to 22.5 million metric tonnes per annum had been commissioned on 31 March 2026. These figures describe the terminal's reported annual handling capacity at that date; they do not represent India's domestic natural gas production or strategic petroleum reserves.

Import dependence is a vulnerability, not automatic proof of insecurity. Its significance depends on supplier concentration, market conditions, alternative sources, transport arrangements, reserves and the ability to respond to disruption.

Prelims focus

  • Jharia is associated with Jharkhand, Talcher with Odisha and Korba with Chhattisgarh.
  • Diversification can concern fuels, suppliers, transport routes and geographical locations.
  • Dahej LNG terminal is located in Bharuch district, Gujarat.
  • Petronet LNG reported the commissioning of Dahej's expansion to 22.5 million metric tonnes per annum on 31 March 2026.
  • Trap: A larger LNG import terminal does not by itself establish greater domestic gas production.

[NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, Chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 24–32; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 76–80; International Energy Agency, ASEAN Energy Security Review, section Energy Security Context, Framework and Overview, consulted 16 November 2026; Petronet LNG Limited, stock-exchange intimation dated 1 April 2026, Commissioning of Additional LNG Regasification Facilities at Dahej.]

pictures.caption: Fuel, supplier, route and geographical diversification address different supply risks.

title: Energy Supply Risks: Import Dependence, Resource Locations and Diversification

body:
Strategic stocks as protection against supply interruptions

Even a well-diversified energy system can face a temporary shortage. Governments may therefore maintain strategic petroleum reserves, which are stocks of crude oil held to help manage serious disruptions in supply. They provide a temporary buffer while alternative supplies are arranged or normal deliveries are restored.

Strategic reserves serve a different purpose from ordinary commercial inventories. Commercial inventories are generally maintained to support routine production, distribution and business operations. Strategic stocks are intended primarily for energy-security emergencies, although storage arrangements may also have commercial components.

India's strategic crude oil facilities

The Government of India established Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL) as the special-purpose vehicle for developing strategic petroleum storage facilities.

In an official statement dated 20 March 2025, the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas reported the following Phase I established storage capacities:

Storage locationStateCapacity (MMT)
VisakhapatnamAndhra Pradesh1.33
MangaluruKarnataka1.50
PadurKarnataka2.50
Total Phase I3 locations5.33

MMT means million metric tonnes. The 5.33 MMT figure is the combined established storage capacity reported by the government, not a statement that exactly 5.33 MMT of crude oil was present in storage on 20 March 2025.

The government had also approved Phase II facilities in July 2021: 4 MMT at Chandikhol in Odisha and 2.5 MMT of additional capacity at Padur in Karnataka, making 6.5 MMT of proposed additional capacity. The 20 March 2025 statement described these as approved facilities, not as already established Phase I storage.

Capacity, inventory and supply coverage are different

  • Storage capacity: The maximum quantity a facility is designed to hold.
  • Actual inventory: The quantity physically stored at a particular time.
  • Days of supply coverage: The period for which available stocks can meet a specified level of consumption or imports.

These quantities are related but cannot be treated as interchangeable. Supply coverage depends on the amount of oil available and the rate at which it is used.

How strategic reserves improve security

If overseas crude shipments are seriously interrupted, a government may authorise the release of strategic stocks under the applicable arrangements. Available crude can then support refinery operations while alternative shipments are secured. The usefulness of this response depends on factors such as accessible inventory, refinery compatibility, transport arrangements and the duration of the disruption.

Strategic reserves cannot eliminate long-term import dependence. Stocks are finite, must eventually be replenished and cannot substitute for adequate refining, transport and distribution infrastructure.

Resilience: withstanding and recovering from shocks

Energy-system resilience is the ability to prepare for disturbances, absorb their effects, recover essential services and adapt to future risks.

Resilience can be improved through emergency fuel stocks, alternative supply routes, reliable infrastructure, suitable backup arrangements, stronger coordination and effective restoration procedures. For electricity, it also involves having sufficient resources to meet demand and maintaining essential services during disturbances. Detailed technical design is separate from these basic principles.

Measures must be chosen for the risk being addressed. Petroleum reserves help with crude-oil interruptions but cannot directly compensate for a failed electricity distribution line. Similarly, additional generating capacity does not automatically solve a fuel transport shortage.

Prelims focus

  • India's strategic petroleum storage programme is implemented through ISPRL.
  • Phase I established capacity reported on 20 March 2025 was 5.33 MMT at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
  • Phase II approval in July 2021 covered 6.5 MMT at Chandikhol and additional storage at Padur.
  • Resilience includes preparation, absorption of shocks, recovery and adaptation.
  • Trap: Approved storage capacity must not be added to commissioned capacity as though both were already operational.

[Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Press Information Bureau, Government Steps to Strengthen Strategic Petroleum Reserves, 20 March 2025; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Press Information Bureau, Two More Commercial-cum-Strategic Facilities of 6.5 MMT Storage Capacity to Be Established under Phase II, 26 July 2021; International Energy Agency, ASEAN Energy Security Review, Energy Security Context, Framework and Overview, consulted 16 November 2026.]
